## The decision this serves

Your PI has budget for four sections and asks how to spend them. Decide now, because
nothing later on this site can rescue a confounded design.

::: {.callout-important}
**Scale.** Runs in about 5 min, peak memory under 1 GB. Watch **pooling sections as
replicates** — that is what stops being valid the moment your sections come from one donor.
:::

## Concept

Spatial experiments are expensive enough that people design them around what fits on a
slide rather than around what they want to test. The result is a class of failure that no
analysis can undo, and which becomes visible only when a reviewer asks what the replicates
were.

### What counts as a replicate

The question sounds pedantic until it costs you a paper. **Pseudoreplication** is treating
samples taken from one experimental unit as independent replicates
[@omics_design_2025]. When units are genuinely independent, no two are expected to be more
similar to each other than any other two — and two sections from the same block fail that
test badly.

Three candidate units, in ascending order of what they buy you:

- **Sections from one block.** These are technical replicates. They tell you about
  sectioning and processing variance. They tell you nothing about biological variability,
  and treating *n* sections as *n* biological replicates inflates your effective sample size
  by a factor of *n* while adding no information about the population.
- **Blocks from one donor.** Capture regional and handling variation within an individual.
  Still one draw from the population you want to generalise to.
- **Donors.** The unit almost every biological claim is implicitly about.

Thousands of spots per section makes this trap easier to fall into, not harder. Spot count
feels like sample size, and the misconception that more data guarantees statistical
validity is exactly what the design literature warns about — it is the number of biological
replicates that determines what you can conclude [@omics_design_2025].

### Confounding, which is the failure that cannot be fixed

Assign one section to control and one to treated, and condition is perfectly aligned with
section. Every difference you observe is real — and is jointly attributable to treatment,
to that particular piece of tissue, to the day it was processed, to its reagent lot, and to
its region of origin. No integration method separates them, because nothing in the data
distinguishes them. This is why lesson 14 says section is batch and batch is confounded
with biology.

The test is arithmetic, not judgement: write the design matrix before the tissue is cut. If
condition and section are collinear, the matrix is singular and the experiment cannot answer
the question. That check costs ten minutes and is worth more than every downstream method on
this site.

Randomisation is the general protection — it is what stops an unmeasured variable lining up
with your comparison [@omics_design_2025]. In practice that means interleaving conditions
across processing batches, slides and days rather than processing all controls on Monday.

### Power, which is not as unavailable as people assume

I would have told you spatial power analysis was unsettled and best skipped. That is out of
date. **PoweREST** estimates power for detecting differentially expressed genes in Visium
experiments, works either before data collection or from preliminary data, and provides both
an R package and a web application [@powerest_2025].

Its approach is worth understanding because it explains why generic power calculators
mislead here. Rather than assuming a Poisson or negative binomial model as bulk and
single-cell tools do, it bootstraps spot-level expression within a region of interest to
generate replicate datasets, then fits a power surface over effect size and detection rate
[@powerest_2025]. The parameter it treats as sample size is the **number of tissue slices**
per group — not the number of spots.

There is also a design question upstream of power that most people never ask: which slices
to cut. Parallel axis-aligned sections tend to yield redundant, correlated information, and
structured batch design can collect more informative samples from fewer slices
[@spatial_design_2024]. Sectioning is destructive, so the ordering of these decisions is not
recoverable.

**The assumption that breaks first.** That a correction step later can separate two
variables you assigned together.

## Runnable notebook

Simulate three allocations of four sections across two conditions and show which questions
each can answer.

Data tier: **Simulated**

::: {.callout-warning}
**Not yet executed.** No output shown and nothing cached.
:::

```{python}
#| label: design-matrices
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

designs = {
    "confounded":  dict(section=[1, 2, 3, 4], condition=["ctl", "ctl", "trt", "trt"],
                        donor=[1, 1, 2, 2]),           # donor == condition too
    "paired":      dict(section=[1, 2, 3, 4], condition=["ctl", "trt", "ctl", "trt"],
                        donor=[1, 1, 2, 2]),           # each donor gives both
    "pseudorep":   dict(section=[1, 2, 3, 4], condition=["ctl", "ctl", "trt", "trt"],
                        donor=[1, 1, 1, 1]),           # one donor, four sections
}

for name, d in designs.items():
    X = pd.get_dummies(pd.DataFrame(d).astype(str), drop_first=True).astype(float)
    rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X.values)
    print(f"{name:<12} columns={X.shape[1]}  rank={rank}  "
          f"{'SINGULAR — cannot separate effects' if rank < X.shape[1] else 'estimable'}")
```

```{python}
#| label: assert-design
# The confounded design must fail. If it does not, the check is not checking.

assert rank["confounded"] < n_cols["confounded"], (
    "a design with condition perfectly aligned to donor should be rank deficient; "
    "if this passes, the encoding is wrong and the check is vacuous"
)
assert rank["paired"] == n_cols["paired"], "the paired design should be estimable"

# Pseudoreplication is NOT caught by rank. It is a variance problem, not a
# collinearity problem, and this assert documents that limitation explicitly.
assert rank["pseudorep"] == n_cols["pseudorep"], (
    "rank deficiency does not detect pseudoreplication — four sections from one "
    "donor give an estimable but meaningless model"
)
```

That last assert is the point of the notebook. The design matrix catches confounding and is
completely blind to pseudoreplication. Rank is necessary, not sufficient.

## Rosetta panel

Design is language-independent, and that is the useful observation: the same model matrix in
R is equally singular. Nothing about the choice of analysis ecosystem rescues an
experimental allocation.

```r
d <- data.frame(
  section   = factor(1:4),
  condition = factor(c("ctl", "ctl", "trt", "trt")),
  donor     = factor(c(1, 1, 2, 2))
)

X <- model.matrix(~ condition + donor, data = d)
qr(X)$rank        # < ncol(X): condition and donor are aliased
alias(lm(rnorm(4) ~ condition + donor, data = d))
```

## Failure mode

**What it produces.** One section per condition, so treatment and section are the same
variable. Every downstream difference is real and uninterpretable, and no integration method
can separate them. The analysis will run perfectly and produce a confident gene list.

**The diagnostic that catches it.** Build the design matrix before the tissue is cut and
check its rank. If it is deficient, the experiment cannot answer the question as posed, and
you learn that while the block is still intact rather than after the sequencing invoice.

## Self-check

### Question 1

What is a replicate in your design — a section, a block, or a donor?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Whichever unit your claim generalises over, and it is almost never the section. Sections
from one block are technical replicates: they quantify sectioning and processing variance,
not biological variability [@omics_design_2025].

If your conclusion is "this happens in disease X," the replicate is the donor, and four
sections from one donor is *n* = 1 regardless of how many spots each contains.
:::

### Question 2

If you dropped your batch correction entirely, what would remain of your effect?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

In a confounded design, everything and nothing — the effect remains, and so does every
alternative explanation for it. Batch correction in that setting does not remove batch, it
removes whichever variance component the algorithm attributes to batch, which includes your
treatment effect because they are the same variable.

If your result depends on the correction, and condition is aliased with section, you have no
result. Lesson 14 covers the measurement side of this.
:::

### Question 3

Which comparison does your allocation make impossible?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Every allocation forecloses something, and the honest move is to name it in advance. Four
sections from two donors, one condition each, forecloses within-donor comparison. Four
sections from one donor forecloses generalisation to the population.

Write the foreclosed comparison in your protocol. It becomes the limitations paragraph you
would otherwise be writing under pressure, months later.
:::

## Going further

What the bench steps do to your data once the design is fixed is lesson 2. The measurement
consequences of section-as-batch are lesson 14.

Formerly omitted, now not: power calculation. PoweREST provides both an R package and a web
application for Visium designs [@powerest_2025], and structured batch design addresses which
slices to cut [@spatial_design_2024]. Neither is a solved problem, but "no tools exist" is
no longer true.
